ref: III.1 (Latin division; ANF ch. 3, first paragraph)
latin: Adicit et aliud: deum semper deum <semper> etiam dominum fuisse, nunquam non dominum. Nullo porro modo potuisse illum semper dominum haberi, sicut et semper deum, si non fuisset aliquid retro semper cuius semper dominus haberetur; fuisse itaque materiam semper deo domino.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: He adds also another point: that as God was always God, there was never a time when God was not also Lord. But it was in no way possible for Him to be regarded as always Lord, in the same manner as He had been always God, if there had not been always, in the previous eternity, a something of which He could be regarded as evermore the Lord. So he concludes that God always had Matter co-existent with Himself as the Lord thereof.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Hermogenes' argument, as Tertullian reports it: God was always God, so he must always have been Lord, so there must always have been something (matter) for him to rule.
use: objection (the Arian-style 'always Lord' argument that Tertullian sets out in order to refute)
limits: Only the opponent's argument is quoted here, not Tertullian's answer. Must be read with III.2-7.

latin: Dei nomen dicimus semper fuisse apud semetipsum et in semetipso, dominum uero non semper. Diuersa enim utriusque condicio: [sed] deus substantiae ipsius nomen, id est diuinitatis, dominus uero non substantiae sed potestatis. Substantiam semper fuisse cum suo nomine quod est deus; postea dominus, accedentis scilicet rei mentio.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: We affirm, then, that the name of God always existed with Himself and in Himself—but not eternally so the Lord. Because the condition of the one is not the same as that of the other. God is the designation of the substance itself, that is, of the Divinity; but Lord is (the name) not of substance, but of power. I maintain that the substance existed always with its own name, which is God; the title Lord was afterwards added, as the indication indeed of something accruing.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: God as a name designates the eternal substance/divinity; 'Lord' names a relation of power and was added later.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (eternal substance; the temporal part is the title, not the essence) and answer to objection
limits: 'Substantiam semper fuisse' is about the substance (deus), not about a distinct eternal person named Son; Tertullian does not here say the Son is coeternal in those words. Bracketed [sed] is editorial.

latin: nam nec pater potuit esse ante filium nec iudex ante delictum. Fuit autem tempus cum ei delictum et filius non fuit quod iudicem et qui patrem dominum faceret. Sic et dominus non ant<e> ea quorum dominus existeret sed dominus tantum futurus quandoque, sicut pater per filium, sicut iudex per delictum, ita et dominus per ea quae sibi seruitura fecisset.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's) [excerpt: from 'nam nec pater' to the end of III.4; 'ant<e>' is an editorial supplement]
english: For He could not have been the Father previous to the Son, nor a Judge previous to sin. There was, however, a time when neither sin existed with Him, nor the Son; the former of which was to constitute the Lord a Judge, and the latter a Father. In this way He was not Lord previous to those things of which He was to be the Lord. But He was only to become Lord at some future time: just as He became the Father by the Son, and a Judge by sin, so also did He become Lord by means of those things which He had made, in order that they might serve Him.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Tertullian says there was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed 'with Him', so that God was not yet Father or Judge, and these titles became his by the Son and by sin.
use: objection (the strongest Arian citation from this treatise); answer to objection only in part: see limits
limits: The sentence is temporal in form ('fuit tempus', 'ante filium'). It is about the names Father and Judge as relations, and III.3 says God's substance is always God; but the plain sense says the Son was not at one time. This is not reconcilable with Nicene eternal generation in its plain wording. Latin reads 'cum ei delictum', NOT 'cum et delictum' as in the brief (see the separate discrepancy item).

latin: Argumentari tibi uideor, Hermogenes? Nauiter scriptura nobis patrocinatur, quae utrumque nomen ei distinxit et suo tempore ostendit. Nam 'deus' quidem, quod erat semper, statim nominat: In principio fecit deus caelum et terram, ac deinceps, quamdiu faciebat quorum dominus futurus erat, 'deus' solummodo ponit: Et dixit deus et fecit deus et uidit deus, et nusquam adhuc 'dominus'. At ubi uniuersa perfecit ... tunc etiam 'dominus' nomen adiunxit: Et accepit deus dominus hominem quem finxit; et praecepit deus dominus Adae.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's) [two cuts marked '...' for length; the Gen. 2:15-16 Latin 'Et accepit deus dominus' is verbatim]
english: Do I seem to you to be weaving arguments, Hermogenes? How neatly does Scripture lend us its aid, when it applies the two titles to Him with a distinction, and reveals them each at its proper time! For (the title) God, indeed, which always belonged to Him, it names at the very first: 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth;' and as long as He continued making, one after the other, those things of which He was to be the Lord, it merely mentions God. 'And God said,' 'and God made,' 'and God saw;' but nowhere do we yet find the Lord. But when He completed the whole creation, and especially man himself ... Then also the Scripture added the name Lord: 'And the Lord God, Deus Dominus, took the man, whom He had formed;' 'And the Lord God commanded Adam.'
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Scripture itself distinguishes the titles: 'God' is used of the eternal God, while 'Lord' appears only after man, when God has something to rule (Gen. 2:15-16).
use: answer to objection (the 'Dominus' names are dated by Scripture, which Tertullian reads as a witness to the temporal character of the title)
limits: Tertullian's argument is about the title 'Lord', not the Son. Its hermeneutic is the title/power distinction of III.3, and it does not itself establish the Son's eternity.

latin: Igitur in quantum putabit ideo materiam semper fuisse quia dominus semper esset, in tantum constabit nihil fuisse, quia constat dominum non semper fuisse. [7] ... Itaque ex quo deus potestatem suam exercuit in eam faciendo ex materia, ex illo materia dominum deum passa demonstrat hoc illum tamdiu non fuisse quamdiu fuit hoc.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: Therefore, in as far as (Hermogenes) shall suppose that Matter was eternal, on the ground that the Lord was eternal, in so far will it be evident that nothing existed, because it is plain that the Lord as such did not always exist. Now I mean also, on my own part, to add a remark for the sake of ignorant persons ... Therefore ever since God exercised His power over it, by creating (all things) out of Matter, although it had all along experienced God as its Lord, yet Matter does, after all, demonstrate that God did not exist in the relation of Lord to it, although all the while He was really so.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: If matter is eternal because the Lord is eternal, then nothing is eternal; the title Lord was not eternal, so the argument fails by its own logic.
use: answer to objection (reductio on the opponent's own premises)
limits: Hermogenes' premise is answered by reductio; Tertullian does not give a positive account of the Son here. The ellipsis '...' marks cut text.

latin: Denique ut necessariam sensit ad opera mundi, statim eam condit et generat in semetipso. Dominus, inquit, condidit me initium uiarum suarum in opera sua: ante saecula fundauit me, priusquam faceret terram, priusquam montes collocarentur; ante omnes autem colles generauit me, prior autem abysso genita sum.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: He immediately creates It, and generates It in Himself. 'The Lord,' says the Scripture, 'possessed me, the beginning of His ways for the creation of His works. Before the worlds He founded me; before He made the earth, before the mountains were settled in their places; moreover, before the hills He generated me, and prior to the depths was I begotten.'
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Tertullian reads Prov. 8:22-25 of the divine Wisdom, which God 'generates in Himself' when he needs her for creation.
limits: Tertullian uses 'generat' of Wisdom as an event tied to the work of creation; he does not in this sentence distinguish eternal from temporal generation.

latin: Agnoscat ergo Hermogenes idcirco etiam sophiam dei natam et conditam praedicari, ne quid innatum et inconditum praeter solum deum crederemus. Si enim intra dominum quod ex ipso et in ipso fuit sine initio non fuit, sophia scilicet ipsius, exinde nata et condita ex quo in sensu dei ad opera mundi disponenda coepit agitari, multo magis non capit sine initio quicquam fuisse quod extra dominum fuerit.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: Let Hermogenes then confess that the very Wisdom of God is declared to be born and created, for the especial reason that we should not suppose that there is any other being than God alone who is unbegotten and uncreated. For if that, which from its being inherent in the Lord was of Him and in Him, was yet not without a beginning,—I mean His wisdom, which was then born and created, when in the thought of God It began to assume motion for the arrangement of His creative works,—how much more impossible is it that anything should have been without a beginning which was extrinsic to the Lord!
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Tertullian says the divine Wisdom was 'born and created' ('natam et conditam'), from the moment God's thought began to move toward creation.
use: objection (strongest temporal wording in this treatise about Wisdom/Word); the defence is that the 'born and created' is said of the Wisdom as a moment of God's planning, to exclude uncreated matter
limits: This is not Nicene wording: Tertullian applies 'natam' and 'conditam' to Wisdom, which he identifies with the Word (XVIII.3), and dates it ('ex quo ... coepit agitari'). Plainly read, it says the Word/Wisdom had a beginning. Tertullian's own aim is to exclude uncreated matter. Say so openly.

latin: Si uero sophia eadem dei sermo est [sensu sophia et], sine quo factum est nihil, sicut et dispositum sine sophia, quale est ut filio dei, sermone unigenito et primogenito, aliquid fuerit praeter patrem antiquius et hoc modo utique generosius, nedum quod innatum <nato> fortius et quod infectum facto ualidius, quia quod, ut esset, nullius eguit auctoris, multo sublimius erit eo quod, ut esset, aliquem habuit auctorem?
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: But if this same Wisdom is the Word of God, in the capacity of Wisdom, and (as being He) without whom nothing was made, just as also (nothing) was set in order without Wisdom, how can it be that anything, except the Father, should be older, and on this account indeed nobler, than the Son of God, the only-begotten and first-begotten Word? Not to say that what is unbegotten is stronger than that which is born, and what is not made more powerful than that which is made.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Wisdom is the Word of God through whom all things were made; so nothing is older or nobler than the Son except the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Son is 'only-begotten and first-begotten', nothing is prior to him but the Father; Word = Wisdom by which all was made, John 1:3)
limits: 'Sermo' here is the Son as Word. Tertullian sets 'Son' against 'matter', not against 'Father'. Bracketed [sensu sophia et] is editorial. Does not settle whether 'born' is eternal.

latin: Ita et hoc nomine materiam deo praeponit Hermogenes, praeponendo eam filio ---- filius enim sermo et deus sermo et Ego et pater unum sumus ----, nisi quod sustinebit aequo animo filius eam praeponi sibi quae patri adaequatur.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's) [the '----' marks are in the source text]
english: Therefore on this ground Hermogenes puts Matter even before God, by putting it before the Son. Because the Son is the Word, and 'the Word is God,' and 'I and my Father are one.' But after all, perhaps, the Son will patiently enough submit to having that preferred before Him which (by Hermogenes), is made equal to the Father!
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Tertullian identifies the Son as the Word, the Word as God (John 1:1), and quotes John 10:30 ('I and my Father are one') as a proof of the Son's equality with the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (John 1:1 and 10:30 applied to the Son; Son equal to the Father in divinity)
limits: Says Matter must not be put 'before the Son' and 'made equal to the Father'. Does not explicitly say 'consubstantial'. Quotations in ANF are marked with footnotes 6313-6314 (John i.1, x.30).

latin: Denique euangelium ut supplementum instrumenti ueteris adhibebo, in quo uel eo magis debuerat ostendi deus ex aliqua materia uniuersa fecisse, quo illic etiam per quem omnia fecerit reuelatur. In principio erat sermo ---- in quo principio scilicet deus fecit caelum et terram ---- et sermo erat apud deum et deus erat sermo. Omnia per illum facta sunt et sine illo factum est nihil.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: In the beginning was the Word—that is, the same beginning, of course, in which God made the heaven and the earth—and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Tertullian quotes John 1:1-3 as the Gospel's witness that God made all things through the Word, not out of matter, and says 'the Word was with God' in the same beginning.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Tertullian's own thesis: the Word was in the beginning, with God, and was God; the Word is the agent of creation)
limits: Tertullian says John's 'in the beginning' is 'the same beginning' as Gen. 1:1 (the beginning of creation), not a prior moment. He does not in this passage use 'Trinity' or 'consubstantial'. The 'In principio erat sermo' is quoted, not argued at length.

latin: At ego sine ullo lenocinio pronuntiationis simpliciter respondebo de omni re posse dici 'erat', etiam de ea quae facta, quae nata sit, quae aliquando non fuerit et quae materia non sit. ... Cui competit prima uerbi positio in definitionem, eiusdem etiam declinatio uerbi decurret in relationem; 'est' definitionis caput, 'erat' relationis facit.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's) [cut marked '...']
english: For of everything which has being, from whatever source it has it, whether it has it by a beginning or without a beginning, the word 'was' will be predicated from the very fact that it exists. ... 'Est' (it is) forms the essential part of a definition, 'erat' (it was) of a relation.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: 'Erat' may be said even of what was created, born, or once was not; 'est' expresses definition and 'erat' expresses relation.
use: answer to objection (grammatical reply to the 'erat' = eternal argument)
limits: This is a grammatical answer about the word 'erat'; it says nothing about the Son's eternal existence, and it does not deal with the Son.

latin: Expedita summa est: nihil inuenio factum nisi ex nihilo, quia quod factum inuenio non fuisse cognosco.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's)
english: The conclusion of the whole is this: I find that there was nothing made, except out of nothing; because that which I find was made, I know did not once exist.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Nothing is made except out of nothing; what is made did not once exist, so matter is not a source of creation.
use: context (the Rule of faith: nothing uncreated except God, creation ex nihilo)
limits: Creation ex nihilo; it does not address the Son.

latin: At enim prophetae et apostoli non ita tradunt mundum a deo factum apparente solummodo et adpropinquante materiae, quia nec materiam ullam nominauerunt, sed primo sophiam conditam, initi[ar]um uiarum in opera[m] ipsius, dehinc et sermonem prolatum per quem omnia facta sunt et sine quo factum est nihil; denique sermone eius caeli confirmati sunt et spiritu ipsius uniuersae uirtutes eorum.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.herm.shtml (read by curl; footer: 'Text edited by J.H. Waszink, 1956'; Latin Library's own chapter [n] numbering; bracketed marks are the editor's) [bracketed letters are the editor's]
english: They did not even mention any Matter, but (said) that Wisdom was first set up, the beginning of His ways, for His works. Then that the Word was produced, 'through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.' Indeed, 'by the Word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all their hosts by the breath of His mouth.'
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: In Scripture Wisdom is set up first and then the Word is 'produced' (prolatum) through whom all things were made; the heavens were established by the Word and the Spirit.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Word 'produced' as agent of creation, with Spirit named beside it); also a Sabellian-style 'prolatio' vocabulary that the Arian reads as temporal
limits: 'Prolatum' is 'sent forth/produced' (Tertullian's word for the Word's going forth), not a sentence about eternity. The Spirit is named in the same breath.

latin: ante omnia enim deus erat solus, ipse sibi et mundus et locus et omnia. solus autem quia nihil aliud extrinsecus praeter illum. ceterum ne tunc quidem solus: habebat enim secum quam habebat in semetipso rationem, suam scilicet. rationalis enim deus, et ratio in ipso prius, et ita ab ipso omnia: quae ratio sensus ipsius est.
latin_edition: Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read by curl). The page names no editor and no edition; the text is not checked against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Evans 1948. Status is therefore PARTLY.
english: For before all things God was alone—being in Himself and for Himself universe, and space, and all things. Moreover, He was alone, because there was nothing external to Him but Himself. Yet even not then was He alone; for He had with Him that which He possessed in Himself, that is to say, His own Reason. For God is rational, and Reason was first in Him; and so all things were from Himself. This Reason is His own Thought (or Consciousness) which the Greeks call λόγος.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: Before creation God had with Him His own Reason (ratio), which is his thought and which is prior; God was not alone.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Reason in God before creation; Word as the Reason uttered later)
limits: Reason, not Son, is what is in God 'before all things'; the Word (sermo) is the uttered Reason. This is a Praxean-facing text and the 'Reason' is the basis for the Son's eternity only if Reason is read as the eternal Son. Tertullian does not say that here.

latin: hanc Graeci lo&gon dicunt, quo vocabolo etiam sermonem appellamus: ideoque iam in usu est nostrorum per simplicitatem interpretationis sermonem dicere in primordio apud deum fuisse, cum magis rationem competat antiquiorem haberi, quia [non] sermonalis a principio sed rationalis deus etiam ante principium, et quia ipse quoque sermo ratione consistens priorem eam ut substantiam suam ostendat.
latin_edition: Latin Library (as V.2); the '&' in 'lo&gon' is the Latin Library's transliteration of λόγον; bracketed [non] is editorial. PARTLY for the same reason as V.2.
english: This Reason is His own Thought (or Consciousness) which the Greeks call λόγος, by which term we also designate Word or Discourse; and therefore it is now usual with our people, owing to the mere simple interpretation of the term, to say that the Word was in the beginning with God; although it would be more suitable to regard Reason as the more ancient; because God had not Word from the beginning, but He had Reason even before the beginning; because also Word itself consists of Reason, which it thus proves to have been the prior existence as being its own substance.
edition: ANF vol. 3 (Coxe ed., Roberts/Donaldson series); printing year not verified; page = ANF original page marked in the archive.org PDF margin
what_it_says: The Word was not 'from the beginning' as a spoken word; Reason was prior; the Word consists of Reason and is its substance.
use: explanation of hard passage (the Word/Reason distinction answers the charge that the Word began at a moment; it is also the source of the 'Word was not from the beginning' wording that Arians cite)
limits: Tertullian's wording 'God had not Word from the beginning' is, read plainly, temporal; the answer is that Reason was eternal and the Word is its uttered form. He does not give a full doctrine of eternal generation here.

what_it_says: The brief quotes III.4 as 'fuit tempus cum et delictum et Filius non fuit'. The text I read (Waszink via Latin Library) reads 'fuit autem tempus cum ei delictum et filius non fuit'.
limits: The brief's wording was not found in the text I read. I did not check Kroymann CSEL 47 or Migne PL 2 (not reached).
memory_only: fuit tempus cum et delictum et Filius non fuit (from the brief, not read in any source this session)

what_it_says: The brief quotes Prax. 5 as 'rationalis Deus ... et in ipso Deo ratio'. The phrase 'in ipso Deo ratio' does not occur in the Latin Library text; the text reads 'rationalis enim deus, et ratio in ipso prius'.
limits: Only one edition (Latin Library) was searched; Kroymann and Evans not reached.

use: answer to objection (to be checked before use)
